name: Dermatology-clinic skin booster regimen

card.summary: Skin-booster injections given at a clinic alongside or after laser, radiofrequency or other energy treatments, aiming at hydrated, smoother-looking skin.
card.note: In-clinic procedures; products and regulatory status vary by country.

quick.overview:
This regimen pairs skin boosters, such as hyaluronic-acid or polynucleotide injectables, with energy-based treatments like fractional laser or RF microneedling. The aim is skin that looks more hydrated, smoother and less red.

Dermatologists who use the pairing say the booster can ease the redness and dryness that follow energy treatments, while the device creates the resurfacing or tightening effect.
quick.how: A clinician performs the energy treatment and gives boosters in the same visit or a short series of visits, with the products and timing chosen by the practitioner. Some clinics apply boosters topically after microneedling instead of injecting.
quick.risks: Risks include redness, swelling, bruising, infection and hypersensitivity. A dermatologist interviewed in Modern Aesthetics said no drug-device combinations are FDA-approved in aesthetic dermatology, and cautioned against unskilled use of products after laser.

lead: The dermatology-clinic skin booster regimen is a combination approach in which skin boosters are used around energy-based treatments such as laser resurfacing, radiofrequency (RF) or microneedling. The energy device resurfaces or stimulates the skin, and the booster is intended to add hydration and support healing.

A 2022 Modern Aesthetics supplement quoted dermatologists describing ways of delivering agents through channels created by lasers and microneedling, including PRP and topical poly-L-lactic acid, and noting that laser-assisted delivery was still at an early stage.[1] One quoted physician said there are no FDA-approved drug-device combinations in aesthetic dermatology.[1]

chain: Energy treatment resurfaces or tightens skin
Booster adds hydration and supports recovery
angle.text: Clinics offer the combination to improve texture, hydration and recovery together. Patients choose it for a smoother, fresher complexion.

infobox: Skin booster plus laser, RF or microneedling
Combination use is not an approved drug-device pairing in the US

paras: Practitioners describe using microchannels from lasers or microneedling to deliver agents such as PRP or poly-L-lactic acid into the skin, applying them right after the treatment while the channels are open.[1] Injected skin boosters and topical boosters are different routes, and clinics vary in which they use.
Proponents say boosters reduce post-treatment redness and add glow. Clinic-published material is the main source of outcome claims.
Quoted dermatologists warn that unskilled practitioners may apply products not intended for the dermis, with infection and hypersensitivity as possible risks, and advise sterile products.[1]
